title: Leading Team Members With an Adversarial Edge
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay addresses colleagues whose default communication style is oppositional across nearly every topic, often without their own awareness of how they come across. It notes these colleagues are frequently bright and valuable, spotting risks others miss, which complicates the leader's response since the trait isn't purely negative. The recommended path is direct, caring feedback about communication style specifically — a category of feedback the piece argues is among the most needed and least often given — paired with an acknowledgment that lasting change may require coaching or style training beyond a single conversation.
points: Notes adversarial colleagues are often unaware of their own default oppositional stance, having developed it over many years.
Complicates the standard response by acknowledging adversarial colleagues frequently make genuinely valuable contributions and spot risks others miss.
Identifies communication-style feedback specifically as among the most needed and least frequently given category of feedback.
Warns that other teammates often respond in kind to an adversarial colleague, escalating friction rather than defusing it.
Recommends direct, caring feedback paired with coaching or style training, acknowledging a single conversation is rarely sufficient for lasting change.
quotes: Some colleagues are testy with everyone and on any topic. They take an adversarial stance as their default position and style.

In many cases, team members with an adversarial edge have no idea about how they come across to their colleagues. The antagonist mindset can become so ingrained as to make people largely unaware of their approach and style.
On the one hand, adversarial colleagues are often quite bright, make valuable contributions, and point out risks or obstacles others miss.
Of the many areas and topics of feedback team members receive from each other and from their leaders, criticism about personal or communication style is perhaps the most needed and least provided.
Coaching, style training, and other forms of assistance may be necessary for a real change to take hold.
